title: Exploring and understanding the support and care needs of people living with advanced bowel cancer and their carers
official: Assessing the Supportive Care needs of patients with advanced colorectal cancer (ACRE)
summary:
Background and study aims
Advanced colorectal cancer can cause many physical, emotional and practical problems for patients and the people who care for them. However, not enough is known about the support that patients and carers need, or whether these needs vary between different groups of patients and different parts of Cheshire and Merseyside.
The ACRE study aims to understand the supportive care needs of people with advanced colorectal cancer and their carers. The study will also look at what support services are available, whether people can access them easily, and whether unmet support needs are linked to increased use of hospital services. The findings will help improve supportive care services for patients and carers across the region.

Who can participate?
1.	Adults aged 18 years and over with advanced colorectal cancer living in Cheshire and Merseyside, including: 1.1. People whose cancer may be removable with surgery but who are considered too frail or unwell for an operation 1.2. People whose cancer has spread and who are receiving palliative treatment 1.3. People whose cancer has spread and who are not receiving palliative treatment
2.	Adults aged 18 years and over who are caring for a patient who meets the above criteria
3.	Healthcare professionals involved in the care of patients with advanced colorectal cancer, including surgeons, oncologists, palliative care doctors and specialist nurses

What does the study involve?
Patients who agree to take part will be asked to complete two questionnaires about their health, symptoms and support needs.
Carers who agree to take part will complete one questionnaire about their own support needs.
Around 100 patients and 100 carers will take part in the questionnaire part of the study. A smaller group of approximately 20 patients and 20 carers will then be invited to take part in an interview. These interviews will explore their experiences of living with advanced colorectal cancer, caring responsibilities, and access to support services.
Interviews can take place face to face, by telephone or online, depending on the participant's preference. Participants may choose to stop an interview, take a break or skip any question they do not wish to answer.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may not receive any direct medical benefit from taking part. However, their experiences could help researchers understand what support patients and carers need and how services could be improved for future patients and families.
The study is considered low risk. Some people may find it upsetting to talk about their illness, care needs or personal experiences. If a participant becomes distressed, they can stop the questionnaire or interview at any time and can be directed to appropriate support services if needed.

Where is the study run from?
The study is coordinated by the University of Liverpool (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 toFebruary 2028.

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by North West Cancer Research (UK).

Who is the main contact?
Ms Dheepa Nair
dnair@liverpool.ac.uk

interventions.name:
A regional, multi-centre, cross-sectional study that will examine, map, describe and understand the patient experience at different stages and in different populations of patients with incurable colorectal cancer.
Using validated questionnaires 100 consenting patients will complete the EORTC-QLQ-CR2

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients:
1.	Patients aged over 18 years with advanced (newly diagnosed and/or recurrent) colorectal cancer from the Cheshire and Merseyside region who belong to one of the following groups:
1.1. Those with potentially resectable cancer for whom surgery would be considered too high risk
1.2. Those with metastatic disease at presentation who are able to receive palliative treatment
1.3. Those with metastatic disease at presentation who are unable to receive palliative treatment
2.	Carers aged over 18 years who are currently caring for a patient who meets the above criteria
3.	Stakeholders with clinical experience in the care of patients with colorectal cancer, including:
3.1. Two colorectal surgical consultants
3.2. Two oncologists
3.3. Two palliative care doctors
3.4. Five palliative care or colorectal nurse specialists

Healthy volunteers are allowed 

Carers over the age of 18  who are currently caring for a patient that fits the above criteria
Exclusion criteria:
Does not meet inclusion criteria
